summary: A 2003 Bytes.com forum thread in which Christoph asks how to return a StringIO containing a complete PIL-altered image (header and pixel data) for use in Zope, since Image.tostring() only returns pixel data. Fredrik Lundh replies with a solution that saves the image to a StringIO buffer in JPEG format and returns getvalue(), which Christoph confirms works. Bengt Richter and JCM briefly debate whether reusing the name 'file' as a variable is advisable, with Richter noting it risks surprises from habit. The thread was closed afterward; the page also contains lots of site boilerplate and unrelated similar-topic listings that were ignored.
one_line: Forum thread on returning a complete in-memory JPEG from a PIL image as a StringIO for Zope, answered by saving to a StringIO buffer.
key_facts: The original question was posted by Christoph on a Bytes.com Python forum thread titled 'PIL: how to return a StringIO of an Image'.
Christoph's script receives an image file from Zope and wants to return a StringIO instance representing the altered image file.
Christoph tried Image.tostring(), but it only returns the pixel data, not the complete file representation with header.
Christoph needed the returned data usable in Zope as an image file, mentioning manage_addImage.
Fredrik Lundh's answer: create file = StringIO(), call image.save(file, "JPEG"), then return file.getvalue().
Christoph replied that the approach was exactly what he wanted and thanked Lundh.
Bengt Richter questioned Lundh's recommendation to use the name 'file' because it shadows a builtin, citing Fredrik Lundh's post dated 14 Nov 2003.
JCM argued that shadowing builtins is allowed because Python is block-structured and new builtins can arrive in any release.
Bengt Richter replied that the main reason to avoid it is to prevent surprises when the habit of using 'file' as a builtin causes errors.
The thread is marked with posts dated Jul 18 '05 and the thread was closed with replies disabled.
The original code example defined modify_image(self, my_image) and used Image.open(my_image) before doing PIL processing.
